summary:
Pernambuco recorded 7 killings of trans and travesti people in 2025, the second-highest count of any Brazilian state in the ANTRA dossier released on 26 January 2026, behind only Ceará and Minas Gerais at 8 each, against a national total of 80. The state's annual figures have fallen from 13 in 2022 to 9 in 2023 and 8 in 2024, so 2025 is the lowest count since 2022, but it remains among the highest in the country.

The danger is concentrated away from Recife. Roughly two-thirds of such killings occur in interior municipalities rather than the state capital, where monitoring, denunciation and access to public policy are weaker, and the recorded victim profile is young (a majority aged 18–29) and overwhelmingly Black (70% of those recorded), travestis and trans women. A trans woman was shot dead inside her home in Belo Jardim, in the Agreste, on 2 October 2025; the Civil Police opened an inquiry to identify the author and motive and no arrests were reported at publication. Fabiana da Silva Lucas, a 30-year-old Black trans woman, was found dead of multiple knife wounds along highway PE-160 in Santa Cruz do Capibaribe on 7 July 2021, the third such killing in Pernambuco that month; the Civil Police told press that a 22-year-old suspect was lynched by locals at the scene.

Over a longer window the same dossier records 83 violent deaths of trans people in Pernambuco across six years, the sixth-highest total nationally for that period, within 349 killings recorded across the Northeast between 2017 and 2025.

No Pernambuco-specific legal restriction or ordinance was identified in the audited sources; the Brazilian national framework applies. Same-sex marriage has been legal nationwide since 2013, the Supreme Federal Tribunal removed the surgical requirement for legal gender change in 2018, and after the Supreme Court's 2019 ruling constitutional and federal criminal provisions prohibit discrimination and hate crimes on sexual-orientation and gender-identity grounds, with transphobia punishable on the same footing as racism. An expat legal guide updated in April 2026 confirms that same-sex marriage, spousal-visa equality and gender-marker rules operate nationwide, so a trans visitor's status and documents are handled on the same footing as anyone else's at entry and in family matters.

Arrest carries a defined placement regime. National Council of Justice Resolution 348 of 13 October 2020, amended by Resolution 366 of 20 January 2021, allows a person to be recognised as LGBTI by self-declaration before a judge, including at a custody hearing; the judge must fix placement in a reasoned decision after consulting the person, set out the available male, female and LGBTI-specific units, and record the declared preference, with later change possible and transfers prioritised where there is violence or a serious threat. LGBTI-specific living spaces may not be used as disciplinary isolation and compulsory transfer as punishment is prohibited. National rules also give LGBTQ prisoners a separate place in prisons, the right to be addressed by social name, placement in women's prisons and the choice of male or female clothing.
tangentialFactors:
Practice does not reliably follow the national detention framework. A peer-reviewed census carried out between April and June 2021 in Rio de Janeiro state prisons interviewed 138 self-declared travesti and trans-woman inmates inside eleven units treated as masculine, documenting housing in masculine-operated units, some in so-called neutral or security units, and treating placement in male units as a double punishment compounded by recurring violations of basic rights. The same study notes a 2015 Rio de Janeiro state law granting parity of treatment with cisgender women in women's units, covering hair length, feminine clothing, accessories and cosmetics, and national norms from 2014 and 2020 permitting people to be housed where they choose.

Protection machinery has widened at national level. An analysis of case law from 2022 records lower courts pressing the Superior Court of Justice toward unanimously extending the remedies of the Maria da Penha Law and the Feminicide Law to trans women, and the 27th Private Chamber of the São Paulo Court of Justice upheld a moral-damage award against a nightclub that refused entry to a trans woman wearing women's clothing, affirming compensation ordered at first instance in Barra Bonita.

Outright International's country overview, updated in March 2026, records that LGBTIQ people still face significant violence and discrimination despite the constitutional and criminal provisions. A May 2024 investigation documented 'boa noite, Cinderela' drink-spiking robberies in which LGBTQIA+ people are targeted in São Paulo nightlife. In the October 2024 municipal elections close to 1,000 transgender candidates stood across every state of the country and received death threats and intimidation, while the number of trans officeholders tripled compared with the previous cycle.
localsOnly:
Same-sex partners have had the right to conjugal visitations in all Brazilian jails since February 2015, under the National Criminal and Penitentiary Council.

Residents of Pernambuco's interior municipalities face the weaker monitoring, slower denunciation and thinner access to public policy that accompany the concentration of killings outside Recife; the state's own six-year total of 83 violent deaths of trans people sits within a Northeast regional count of 349 killings between 2017 and 2025.

No placement rule, special unit, segregation practice or documented case issued by the Secretaria de Administração Penitenciária e Ressocialização de Pernambuco was located in the audited sources, so state corrections practice is governed by the national Council of Justice resolutions rather than by any sourced state instrument.
outOfScopeNotes:
Whether Pernambuco's courts or prosecutors have applied the 2019 hate-crime provisions in any trans case is unresolved: no state-level enforcement record, charge or conviction was sourced.

The outcome of the Belo Jardim inquiry opened after the killing of 2 October 2025 is unresolved; the report available records no arrests at publication and nothing later was sourced.

The exact period covered by the figure of 83 violent deaths of trans people in Pernambuco over six years is not specified in the source, and the sixth-place national ranking for that window could not be verified against a full state-by-state table.

No Pernambuco-specific ordinance, municipal rule or state prison placement instruction was found in the audited sources; the absence of such a rule in the inventory is not evidence that none exists.

Whether the ANTRA state counts capture killings only inside Pernambuco's borders, and how the count treats cases with an unresolved motive, is not addressed in the sources reviewed.
